The Helan Mountains, sometimes called a "mountain island in the sky," wall off two very different worlds: the semi-arid Ordos Plateau and Yellow River Valley on one side, the arid desert of the Alxa Plateau on the other. Like the ranges of western North America's Great Basin, the Helan Range isolates dense conifer forests and may shelter endemic plants and animals found nowhere else. Scientists have barely studied this ecoregion, yet it holds several rare species: blue sheep, blue-eared pheasants, and the endemic Helan pika. Logging still chips away at the habitat, and the region's high biological diversity hangs in the balance.

We derived a time-dependent mild-slope equation, starting from the formal derivation of Smith & Sprinks (1975). From there we got the higher-order dispersion relation for waves over an uneven bottom.

Then, using only the linear dispersion for steady waves, we recovered equation (2.12) of Chamberlain & Porter (1995), the Modified Mild-Slope Equation (MMSE). The leading-order solution shows the modified curvature terms of the MMSE matter, while the slope square terms stay negligible, as the mild-slope assumption requires. So we kept every modified curvature term the MSE drops. That gave us a uniform model.

We built a numerical model with the finite element method (FEM) to predict wave scattering by a varying bottom. In general, the uniform model predicts the main features of waves over various sea beds, including sinusoidal beds and man-made bars. On sinusoidal beds, it matches the experimental data more closely than other established models. On man-made bars, both the MMSE and the uniform model match the data more closely than Kirby (1986).

The FEM model also applies to the transformation of waves over arbitrarily-varying bathymetry.

UPO-06: prhI Gene Synthesis
UPO-06 carries the coding sequence for *Ralstonia solanacearum* prhI, the ECF sigma factor you need for transcription driven by the Prh signal transduction system. PrhR activates the gene, and it then directs sigma factor expression by switching on the PprhJ promoter. We optimized the sequence for expression in *Escherichia coli*.

UPO-11: PprhJ Promoter Synthesis
UPO-11 gives you the PprhJ promoter region. It responds to plant cell contact through signal transduction mediated by PrhA and PrhR, and PrhI activates it. We optimized this sequence for expression in *Escherichia coli* as well.

Look at Fig. 15 and you'll see the alitrunk is conspicuously swollen, sitting much higher than the propodeal dorsum. The propodeum carries a pair of strong spines, straight to slightly upcurved. There's no metanotal groove. The metapleural lobes are triangular and conspicuous.

In profile, the petiole shows an elongate peduncle and a well-developed node whose dorsum slopes down posteriorly, leaving a short posterior face. On the postpetiole, the anterior and dorsal surfaces form a single convexity, and the posterior face is truncated. From above, the nodes of both petiole and postpetiole are broader than long.

Now the head. Its dorsum is strongly longitudinally rugose, with 5–7 rugae between the frontal carinae at eye level. These rugae are irregular and meander slightly, and you'll usually find a few anastomoses. The scrobal area is largely smooth, though it usually carries 1–2 fine rugulae crossing its width just behind the antennal fossa. Behind the eyes, the sides of the head are finely reticulate-rugose, and that sculpture runs around the posterior margins of the scrobe to the occiput. Between the rugae, the spaces are unsculptured, or at most show faint superficial traces.

The dorsal alitrunk is finely but strongly reticulate-rugose everywhere, with broad shining interspaces. The petiole dorsum is rugulose. The postpetiole ranges from rugulose to only faintly sculptured, and the gaster is unsculptured. Every dorsal surface of head and body is densely clothed with fine, acute hairs. Color runs from dark reddish brown to blackish brown.

Subject: A Note on Buraq

People once lived comfortably in a world where reality and myth overlapped. Modern comparative biology drew a hard line between them. But the line never erased the middle ground where Buraq lives. We need figures like her to hold empirical knowledge and spiritual experience together.

She still does that work in contemporary culture, standing between rationalist taxonomies and the old pull of myth. Here's something worth knowing about early hearing development. Children typically develop spoken language in their first few years. If hearing is impaired, a child can lose both the ability to speak and the ability to understand speech.

Often, nobody notices a severely hearing-impaired (deaf) child has a hearing deficit until communication problems have already strained the family and slowed social skills. If that child grows up in a Deaf community using sign language instead of spoken language, those problems shrink (please see our article on Deaf Culture).

That's why many developed countries test newborns' hearing, so a deaf child isn't accidentally isolated in a hearing family. Sign language is a full means of communication, but literacy depends on understanding speech. In most written language, the sound of a word is coded in symbols.

Someone who hears well enough to learn to speak and read keeps that ability even if hearing later fades. But a person who never heard well enough to learn to speak rarely reads proficiently (see [4]). Most evidence points the same way: identify hearing impairment early, and a child with very insensitive hearing has the best chance of learning spoken language. Listening matters for learning a second language, too.

Transduction is how physical and chemical signals get converted into neural impulses. In the nervous system, it's the process of translating stimuli into electrical signals. In sensory transduction, specialized sensory receptors transform physical or chemical inputs into electrical impulses that travel to the brain.

The visual system shows how this works. In the retina, rod and cone cells bridge the physical environment and neural communication. When light strikes these photoreceptors, it changes the shape of the protein rhodopsin. That shift sets off a cascade of events that alters the electrochemical gradient of the photoreceptor. As the gradient drops, the electrical signals sent to the brain decrease. So more light hitting the photoreceptor means fewer electrical impulses, and that's how your brain decodes the visual world with precision.

Here's what our analysis of lung tissue volume and functional changes found.

We calculated total lung tissue volume as: number of voxels × volume of the voxel, for any compartment with a CT number above zero.

PEEP withdrawal changed functional residual capacity (ΔFRC), which we computed as the difference in total gas volume in the whole lung between PEEP and ZEEP. We defined alveolar derecruitment as the difference in gas volume within poorly aerated and nonaerated regions between those same conditions.

We also tracked how gas volume changed from PEEP withdrawal in normally aerated regions, meaning CT attenuations between -500 and -900 HU (see Figure 2).

Subject: Tips for Hitchhiking in the Ruhr Area, Germany

Dear Customer,

The Ruhr Area (German: Ruhrgebiet), or just the Ruhr, is an urban region in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It's a cluster of former industrial cities: Duisburg, Oberhausen, Bottrop, Mülheim an der Ruhr, Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Herne, Hamm, Hagen, Dortmund, Recklinghausen, Unna, and Witten.

About five million people live here. That's significantly more than Berlin, Hamburg, or Munich. The motorway density is high, yet hitchhiking is harder than you'd expect, because the minor roads form a confusing network. The motorways that matter are the A1, A2, and A3.

If you're hitching here, stay on those three. The smaller roads will strand you; hardly any transit traffic passes through them. Germany is generally a pleasant country for hitchhiking, but the Ruhr Area is its most unpleasant corner for it. Hitching inside the Ruhr feels like hitching in Istanbul; the cities are independent, but to a traveler they blur into districts of one massive city.

We hope this helps you plan your trip safely and enjoyably.

Mobile Gaming: The Next Evolution of Co-Creation

Mobile internet is expanding what storytelling can do, through electronic games that run on portable, location-aware interfaces. It's the latest step in a decades-long evolution of games that make the player a co-author alongside the original designers, not just an avatar in the gameworld.

Location-aware interfaces let you pull real places into your gameworld, and push the gameworld back out into real places. No earlier interactive media could do that. Mobile games also drop linear narratives. Their storytelling is cooperative, and it depends on how you experience the place you're standing in.

The "author-player" idea isn't new. But mobile games push it past the limits of traditional video games, because the worldmaking extends past the screen. The interface turns what you see, hear and feel in a real place into a storytelling tool.

In our essay, we theorize the unique storytelling potential of mobile games and describe our experience trying to realize it: we designed and built a hybrid-reality game called University of Death.
